channel.title: Protocol STAMP
channel.description: An independent program that measures whether an AI can be made to show its receipts. Issues on alternate Saturdays at 15:37 America/Chicago; The Bench on Mondays and Thursdays. Protocol STAMP can make mistakes; verify before you implement anything, and see https://protocolstamp.com/corrections/ for what we have already got wrong.

item.title: The Calibration Vol 003 · Sat20261003
item.description: Are the judges right? One person labelled 87 draws blind; every judge is scored against him. The judges agree with each other more than with the person, and the decision models catch least. Build af3906b9d9ad.

item.title: The Calibration Vol 002 · Sat20261003
item.description: Does the judging hold? A judge from another family, the panel on a second model, and two decision models, tested against the panel under a signed pre-registration. Build ae993179f05f.

item.title: The Bench Vol 003 · Five Cases, a Hundred Times Each
item.description: LangChain reported that Jev, a new decision model, matched a human reviewer on all 500 pass/fail decisions it judged. The 500 were five cases repeated a hundred times. What that can carry, the open models that followed, and the seven rules any judge must pass before it grades our work.

item.title: The Bench Vol 002 · Something It Can Actually Check
item.description: Four Claude models were handed a record with two errors planted in it, twice - once with web search off, once with it on. All twelve cells caught both. Retrieval changed nothing about that, and everything about what could honestly be said afterwards.

item.title: The Bench Vol 001 · The No. 1 Complaint
item.description: Is hallucination really what people hate most about AI? The review data says yes. Then thirteen AI models were asked the same question, word for word, and the answer that came back was that our own table was wrong. It was, nine times over.

item.title: Stop marking it like a student
item.description: A model guesses when your question looks like it wants help, and hedges when it looks like it might cause harm. Neither behavior is about what the model knows. Both are about how it is marked.

item.title: Why "I don't know" can be a lie
item.description: Most prompt hygiene guards against invention and stops there. The case for treating abstention as a symmetric failure, and what it costs to guard only one side.
